questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: AeroLumen, a regional airline, runs a customer service agent built with the Claude Agent SDK. Through the app's chat, it handles refunds, rebookings, and baggage issues using internal MCP tools: get_passenger, lookup_booking, verify_identity, process_refund, rebook_flight, and escalate_to_human. Business constraints: no booking change or refund may happen before identity verification; refunds above R$ 2,000 require human approval; personal data is subject to LGPD; the goal is to resolve 70% of cases without a human, with no unnecessary escalations.

During the monthly audit, the team discovers that in about 2% of conversations the agent called process_refund before verify_identity, even though the system prompt states, in capital letters, that verification is mandatory. What is the most appropriate fix?
opcoes: Reinforce the system prompt with three few-shot examples showing the correct call order and repeat the rule at the end of the prompt, where it gets more attention.
A PreToolUse hook that intercepts process_refund and returns permissionDecision "deny", with a reason, as long as the session has no successful verify_identity on record.
A daily job in which a second model reviews the day's transcripts and flags refunds issued without verification, for manual reversal.

A PostToolUse hook on process_refund that checks, right after the call, whether identity verification occurred in the session and, if it did not, returns an error message to the model asking it to verify.
questoes.explicacao: Financial/compliance consequence → programmatic enforcement before execution (PreToolUse with deny). Prompts and few-shot are best-effort; after-the-fact auditing and PostToolUse come too late.
feedbacks: Tempting because it usually lowers the error rate. But it remains probabilistic (anti-pattern 3: critical rule only in the prompt). Going from 2% to 0.5% still means refunds without verified identity.
Correct. A rule with financial and compliance consequences needs deterministic enforcement. The hook always blocks, and the returned reason guides the model to verify identity first.
It detects the problem after the money is already gone. It's auditing, not prevention, and it's more complex than necessary.
Event trap: PostToolUse runs after the tool has executed, so the refund has already been processed. The block has to happen before execution, in PreToolUse.

questoes.pergunta: In the AeroLumen agent, long conversations (40+ turns, multiple flights and partial refunds) go through automatic context summarization. After that, the agent starts citing mixed-up booking references and rounded amounts ("about R$ 1,800" instead of R$ 1,837.40). What fixes the root cause?
opcoes: Maintain a case facts block (booking references, exact amounts, dates, IDs) that is never summarized and is sent on every turn.
Instruct the summarizer, in the compaction prompt, to preserve all numbers, booking references, and identifiers exactly, without rounding or paraphrasing any value.
Migrate to a model with a 1M-token window and turn off summarization, keeping the full history.
Have the agent call lookup_booking again before every response to reload the booking data.
questoes.explicacao: Case facts: exact amounts, dates, and IDs live in a block that is never summarized.
feedbacks: Correct. Summarization loses precisely amounts, dates, and IDs. A case facts block that is never paraphrased preserves the exact data no matter how many times the rest is compressed.
Tempting, and it even helps, but it is probabilistic: the summary is still a paraphrase and can still round or mix up values. It doesn't guarantee what needs to be exact.
Attacks the wrong symptom: a larger window costs all the tokens on every turn and worsens lost in the middle; the exact data would be buried in the middle of an enormous conversation.
Spends calls and context on every turn and doesn't cover facts that came from the conversation (agreed amounts, partial refunds already settled). Noise instead of a stable record.

questoes.pergunta: At AeroLumen, a passenger writes in all caps, swears, and threatens to expose the company on social media because the seat selection fee (R$ 38) was charged twice. The policy allows duplicate fees to be reversed automatically. An analyst proposes escalating every conversation whose sentiment score falls below -0.7. What is the best course of action?
opcoes: Escalate based on the sentiment score, because a very angry customer poses reputational risk and deserves priority human service.
Ask the model to report its confidence from 0 to 1 in the resolution and escalate when it falls below 0.8.
Resolve it: confirm the duplicate charge and reverse the fee through the normal flow, without escalating.
Respond with empathy first and, if the sentiment score doesn't improve within two turns, automatically escalate to a supervisor.
questoes.explicacao: Sentiment ≠ complexity. Escalate on an explicit request, a policy exception/gap, or lack of progress.
feedbacks: Anti-pattern 5: escalating on sentiment. High anger doesn't make the problem hard; the human would issue the same reversal, just later.
Anti-pattern 4: self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated; the model may say 0.95 while wrong or 0.6 while right. It is not a reliable escalation criterion.
Correct. Sentiment is not complexity: the case is simple and covered by policy. Escalating here only lengthens the queue and the resolution time.
Seems balanced, but it still uses sentiment as the trigger. The criterion should be the nature of the problem (covered by policy, progress), not the customer's mood.

questoes.pergunta: AeroLumen wants explicit criteria for immediate escalation by the agent. Which situations should trigger escalate_to_human right away? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: The passenger is furious about a baggage fee charged in accordance with the fare they purchased and threatens to cancel their loyalty program membership.
The passenger, calm and polite, requests a full refund of a non-refundable fare citing a hospitalization, a situation the current policy does not cover.
The model reports a confidence of 0.42 in its own classification of the issue type.
The passenger writes "I want to talk to a person" in their second message, before the agent has tried anything.
The conversation has passed 25 turns, but the agent keeps making progress: it has already rebooked two segments and one remains.
questoes.explicacao: Immediate triggers: an explicit request for a human and a policy exception/gap. Sentiment, self-reported confidence, and conversation length are not.
feedbacks: Strong sentiment with a simple, covered case: the agent explains the fare rule. Escalating would be anti-pattern 5.
Correct. Policy exception/gap: the agent has no authority to create a new rule. A calm tone doesn't change that.
Anti-pattern 4: self-reported confidence is not calibrated. The way forward is to ask/clarify, not to escalate.
Correct. An explicit request for a human is an immediate trigger; insisting on resolving it first goes against the customer.
Conversation length is not a criterion; there is progress. The correct trigger is lack of progress after reasonable attempts.

questoes.pergunta: In the AeroLumen agent, the MCP wrapper for lookup_booking catches any exception and returns [] so as "not to break the agent". During a traffic peak, the booking backend timed out and the agent told dozens of passengers that "no booking exists with that booking reference". What is the correct redesign?
opcoes: Instruct the agent, whenever it receives an empty list, to call lookup_booking two more times before concluding that the booking doesn't exist.
A search that ran and found nothing → success with an empty list; timeout → structured error (transient, isRetryable true).
Make the wrapper try three times with backoff and, if all attempts fail, return an empty list as usual.
Replace the [] with an "Operation failed" string with isError true and no other fields, so the agent knows something went wrong.
questoes.explicacao: An empty result is information; a timeout is a failure. Structured error with category and retryability.
feedbacks: Treats the symptom: it also retries legitimate empty results (a mistyped booking reference), and the timeout is still indistinguishable from "not found".

Correct. Empty ≠ failure. The model needs to know whether the search ran; with a structured transient error it can retry or tell the passenger the system is unstable, without asserting something false.
A local retry for transient errors is good, but ending with an empty list is still silent suppression (anti-pattern 7): the agent keeps claiming the booking doesn't exist.
Better than hiding it, but it's a generic error (anti-pattern 6): with no category or isRetryable, the model doesn't know whether to retry, fix the input, or escalate.

questoes.pergunta: At AeroLumen, a passenger requests a refund for a Light fare ticket, which is non-refundable by contract. How should process_refund respond so that the agent reacts well?
opcoes: A validation error, indicating that the fare_class field is not accepted, so the agent corrects the input and tries again.
A transient error with isRetryable true, so the agent tries again later in case the policy changes.
Success with a refunded amount of R$ 0.00, letting the agent infer from the amount that the fare is non-refundable.
A structured business error: isRetryable false, the rule violated, and an alternative (travel credit).
questoes.explicacao: Categories: transient (retry), validation (fix the input), business (explain/escalate), permission (escalate).
feedbacks: Wrong category: the input is correct; what blocks it is the policy. Labeling it as validation leads the model to "fix" the request and try again.
Policy is not service instability. Marking it as retryable produces useless retries and false promises to the customer.
Masks a refusal as a success. The model may report "refund processed" and the customer ends up confused. A business failure must be explicit.
Correct. A business error is not retryable; with the rule and the alternative in the result, the agent explains the policy to the customer and offers the credit instead of insisting.

questoes.pergunta: At AeroLumen, escalate_to_human currently sends only "customer needs help with refund". The human support reps, who can't see the chat, complain that they have to ask all the questions again. What is the best change?
opcoes: Attach the full conversation transcript, with the tool results, to the ticket so the rep has all the context available without losing any detail.
Before transferring, ask the passenger to describe the problem again in their own words to record it in the ticket.
Pass the session ID to the rep so they can reopen the conversation in the dashboard and read the history when needed.
A structured summary: identity, booking reference, problem, actions taken, reason for the blocker, recommendation, and amount.
questoes.explicacao: Handoff = structured summary (customer, problem, actions, blocker, recommendation, amount).
feedbacks: Tempting ("nothing gets lost"), but it dumps 40 turns on the human, who won't read them. What's missing is organized synthesis, not volume.
Shifts the work onto the customer and worsens the experience; the agent already has the information.
Only gives access to the same long history; it doesn't solve the problem of having to reconstruct the case.
Correct. The human usually doesn't read the transcript; a structured handoff leaves the case ready for a decision with no rework.

questoes.pergunta: The AeroLumen agent has grown to 17 tools (baggage, miles, refunds, rebooking, seats, FAQ, pets...) and the wrong-tool rate has gone up, especially among tools from neighboring domains. What is the best architecture?
opcoes: Rewrite the 17 descriptions stating when to use each tool, with an input example and how it differs from the neighboring tools in the same domain.
A coordinator routing to specialized subagents, each with 4 to 5 tools from its own domain.
Set tool_choice "any" to force the agent to always call some tool before responding.
Raise effort to "max" so the model reasons more before choosing the tool.
questoes.explicacao: Too many tools in a single agent → split into specialized subagents with 4–5 tools each.
feedbacks: It's the first thing to try with 2–3 overlapping tools, but with 17 tools improving the descriptions alone isn't enough (anti-pattern 8).
Correct. With ~17 tools, selection degrades; splitting into specialists keeps few tools visible at decision time, which is the guideline.
Forcing a call doesn't improve the choice of which one to call; and on newer models "any" may not even be accepted.
More reasoning doesn't make up for a large, overlapping decision space; it costs more and attacks the symptom.

questoes.pergunta: In the AeroLumen agent's loop, the code ends the turn as soon as the response contains a text block. Logs show responses like "I'll check your booking now." followed by a tool_use that never gets executed. What is the fix?
opcoes: Decide based on stop_reason: "tool_use" executes the tools and continues; "end_turn" ends the turn.
Detect phrases like "I'll check" or "one moment" and, in those cases, keep the loop open.
Instruct the model, in the system prompt, to never write text in the same response in which it calls a tool.
Keep the current rule and add a 10-iteration limit as the main stopping criterion.
questoes.explicacao: stop_reason drives the loop; text + tool_use in the same response is normal.
feedbacks: Correct. content can mix text and tool_use; having text doesn't mean it's done. stop_reason is what decides.
Anti-pattern 1: deciding the end of the loop by reading natural language. It breaks with any variation in phrasing.
Tries to change the model's legitimate behavior via the prompt instead of fixing the code; and it remains fragile.
Anti-pattern 2: an iteration limit is a backstop, not the main mechanism; and it doesn't fix the ignored tool_use.

questoes.pergunta: In the AeroLumen agent, get_passenger ("fetches passenger data") and search_customer ("looks up customer information") come from different teams, and the model alternates between them inconsistently. Which fixes address the root cause? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Add an intent classifier in front of the agent, trained on labeled conversations, that decides which of the two tools should be used for each passenger message.
Force tool_choice to get_passenger on every first turn of the conversation.
Put 30 example customer messages in the system prompt, each with the correct tool.
Merge the two into a single tool with an explicit lookup-key parameter (CPF, email, or loyalty number), eliminating the overlap.
If they must exist separately, rename them by purpose and state in the description when to use each one and how it differs from the other.
questoes.explicacao: Overlap → merge, or separate them with differentiating names and descriptions.
feedbacks: A more complex solution than necessary: an extra component to compensate for poor descriptions.
Forces a fixed choice even when it doesn't fit, and on newer models forcing may return a 400.
Lots of examples, memorized, to patch the overlap; it doesn't generalize and it bloats the prompt.
Correct. Overlapping tools cause misrouting; merging removes the ambiguity at the root.
Correct. The description is the selection criterion; explicitly differentiating the neighboring tools is the simplest fix when both are needed.

questoes.pergunta: The AeroLumen agent has a 14,000-token system prompt (policies) and stable tools, but usage.cache_read_input_tokens stays at zero on every request. Which causes explain this? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: The user message changes every turn, because each passenger writes something different.
Four cache_control breakpoints were used (tools, system, history, and last message), which is the maximum allowed by the API.
The first line of the system prompt is "Current date and time: {now}", filled in on every request.
Requests arrive every 20 seconds, well within the default 5-minute TTL.
The tools array is built from a set whose order varies between runs and according to the passenger's loyalty tier.
questoes.explicacao: Stable first, volatile last; timestamps and nondeterministic tools are silent invalidators.
feedbacks: The volatile part after the last breakpoint can change freely; that is exactly the correct design.
Four is the allowed limit, not a problem. Using breakpoints doesn't invalidate the cache.
Correct. A timestamp in the prefix changes on every request and invalidates everything from that point on.
Frequent requests within the TTL are the ideal scenario for cache reads.
Correct. The cache matches the exact prefix in the order tools → system → messages; tools that vary in order or content invalidate the cache.

questoes.pergunta: AeroLumen enabled server-side compaction on the agent for very long sessions. After the first compaction event, the agent starts acting as if the conversation had started from scratch. The integration code appends only the response text (the "text" blocks) to the history. What is the fix?
opcoes: Append the entire response.content to the history, including the compaction block, not just the text.
Replace compaction with context editing using clear_tool_uses, which removes only old tool results and therefore better preserves the conversation's narrative.
Use the memory tool to write the entire transcript on every turn and reread it on the next turn.
Turn off compaction and increase max_tokens so the responses can hold more context.
questoes.explicacao: With compaction, send back the complete response.content; append-only history.
feedbacks: Correct. The compacted summary comes in its own block; by keeping only the text, the compaction state is silently lost and the earlier context disappears.
Context editing clears old tool results; it doesn't summarize the narrative. And it doesn't fix the bug of discarding blocks from the response.
Memory is for findings across sessions, not for patching a badly assembled history; rereading the entire transcript undoes the benefit of compaction.
max_tokens limits the output, not the input window. It confuses the two ceilings.

questoes.pergunta: AeroLumen's get_passenger is an MCP server from an external vendor and returns 40 fields, including the full card number and passport number. The team wants the model to receive only the necessary fields, with PII masked, without depending on the vendor. What is the right mechanism?
opcoes: Instruct in the system prompt that the agent must never repeat card numbers, passport numbers, or other sensitive data to the passenger, even when the passenger explicitly asks.
A PreToolUse hook on get_passenger that removes the sensitive fields from the call.
Enable context editing to clear old get_passenger results after a few turns.
A PostToolUse hook that filters the fields and masks the card and passport numbers before the model sees the result.
questoes.explicacao: PostToolUse: normalize, trim fields, and mask PII before the model sees it.
feedbacks: The data has already entered the context; the prompt only tries to keep it from leaking, probabilistically (anti-pattern 3).
PreToolUse acts on the call's input, before any result exists; there is nothing to mask there.
It clears the results after the model has already read the 40 fields with PII; it doesn't prevent exposure or slim down the current decision.
Correct. PostToolUse deterministically normalizes and cleans results; it slims down the context and protects PII.

questoes.pergunta: In one turn, the AeroLumen agent emitted two tool_use blocks in the same response (lookup_booking and get_passenger). The code executes both and sends each tool_result in a separate user message; when lookup_booking fails, it simply doesn't send a result for it. What is wrong?
opcoes: The correct approach is to set disable_parallel_tool_use to true, because parallel calls are not supported with MCP tools.
All tool_result blocks in a single user message, with the exact tool_use_ids; the failed one goes with is_error true.
The sending is fine; the only thing missing is, when a tool fails, ending the loop and asking the passenger to try again later.
The separate messages are right, since each tool has its own cycle; the only problem is that the failed tool should get an empty tool_result.
questoes.explicacao: Parallel: all tool_results in one user message, exact ids, failure with is_error.
feedbacks: Parallel calls are supported; disabling them only hides the assembly bug and makes the service slower.
Correct. Parallel tool use: one result per tool_use_id, all together; omitting the failed one leaves the call unanswered and prevents the model from reasoning about recovery.
Aborting the flow because of one failure wastes the result that succeeded; the model should receive the error and decide.
An empty result for a failure is silent suppression; and separate messages break the expected pairing.

questoes.pergunta: The team developing the AeroLumen agent uses Claude Code and wants a "transcript auditor" subagent with its own prompt, restricted to reading (Read, Grep, Glob), available to all developers in the repository. Where and how should it be defined?
opcoes: In ~/.claude/agents/auditor.md on each developer's machine, with the same frontmatter.
In .claude/agents/auditor.md, version-controlled, with frontmatter defining description, allowed tools, and its own prompt.
Use the built-in Explore subagent, which is already read-only, and paste the audit prompt into CLAUDE.md.
As a section in the project's CLAUDE.md describing the auditor role and asking Claude not to edit files while auditing.
questoes.explicacao: The team's custom subagent → version-controlled .claude/agents/, tools in the frontmatter.
feedbacks: Works for whoever configured it, but it's personal: it isn't shared or version-controlled with the team.
Correct. Custom subagents live in .claude/agents/ (project-level, shared via git), with restricted tools in the frontmatter.
Explore is read-only, but it doesn't carry a role of its own; mixing audit instructions into CLAUDE.md pollutes every session.
It doesn't create an isolated subagent, and the read-only restriction exists only in the prompt; it isn't deterministic.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: the law firm Andrade & Teles Advogados uses a multi-agent system to produce due diligence reports on M&A transactions. A coordinator receives the request (target company, period, scope) and delegates to research subagents (public records and lawsuits, news, financial analysis) and to a synthesis subagent. Constraints: every claim in the report needs a source and a date; conflicts between sources must be surfaced to the partners; the report must be delivered within 4 hours.

The coordinator delegates with prompts like "Analyze the target company's risks". The subagents return generic text, sometimes about a different company with a similar name. What is the best fix?
opcoes: Increase the subagents' max_turns so they have more iterations to figure out on their own which company is meant.
Allow the subagents to query each other directly to agree on which company is the target.
Add to the subagents' system prompt the instruction "always confirm you are researching the correct company before starting any search".
Pass the legal name, CNPJ, period, scope, findings so far, and output format in the delegation prompt.
questoes.explicacao: Subagents don't inherit context: pass everything explicitly in the delegation prompt.
feedbacks: More iterations don't bring in information that was never passed; they only increase cost and the chance of picking the wrong company.
Subagents talking to each other breaks hub-and-spoke; the problem is that the coordinator doesn't pass the context.
Asking for confirmation without providing the data (CNPJ, legal name) doesn't help: the subagent has nothing to confirm against.
Correct. The subagent's context is isolated: it doesn't inherit the coordinator's history. Everything it needs must go in the prompt.

questoes.pergunta: In the Andrade & Teles system, the three research subagents are independent of one another, but the log shows the coordinator calling one Agent per turn, waiting for each to finish. The report takes 3h40. Which change reduces the time without altering the architecture?
opcoes: Have the coordinator emit the three Agent calls in the same response, so they run in parallel.
Send the three research tasks through the Batch API, which processes requests in parallel at a 50% discount.
Create three coordinators, each responsible for one subagent, running in separate processes.
Lower each subagent's max_tokens so that each one finishes faster.
questoes.explicacao: Multiple Agent calls in the same coordinator response = parallel execution.
feedbacks: Correct. Parallelism comes from multiple Agent calls in the same response; separate turns are sequential.
Batch has no SLA and can take up to 24h; and it doesn't support each subagent's multi-turn tool loop.
Unnecessary complexity, and it loses the single point of aggregation and error handling.
Cuts outputs off midway (stop_reason max_tokens) and doesn't change the sequential execution.

questoes.pergunta: For a request about the target company's "regulatory risks" (pharmaceutical industry), the Andrade & Teles coordinator decomposed it only into "ANVISA registrations". The report omitted relevant environmental violations and labor liabilities. What is the most appropriate fix?
opcoes: Instruct the synthesis subagent to be comprehensive and cover every possible regulatory risk in the sector, leaving no area out of the final report.
Increase the number of results the public records subagent returns per search.
Broaden the decomposition and check coverage against an explicit list of the sector's regulatory areas.
Run the entire pipeline twice and merge the results of the two runs.
questoes.explicacao: Narrow decomposition → broaden it and check coverage explicitly.
feedbacks: Without research on the omitted areas, the synthesis can only make things up or stay generic; the problem originated in the decomposition.
More results about ANVISA are still about ANVISA; it doesn't cover the areas that were never delegated.
Correct. The decomposition is too narrow; the fix is to broaden the decomposition and verify coverage explicitly.
Repeating the same narrow decomposition produces the same gaps, at twice the cost.

questoes.pergunta: To save tokens, an Andrade & Teles engineer proposes that the financial subagent send findings directly to the litigation subagent, bypassing the coordinator. What is the correct assessment?
opcoes: Reject it: in hub-and-spoke, all communication goes through the coordinator.
Accept it, as long as the subagents use the same JSON message format to avoid misunderstandings.
Accept it, because it reduces the context load on the coordinator, which is the system's bottleneck.
Accept it only for high-risk findings, which need to reach the other subagent faster.
questoes.explicacao: Hub-and-spoke: all communication goes through the coordinator.
feedbacks: Correct. Direct communication between subagents is an anti-pattern: it loses traceability, central error handling, and control over what gets passed along.
The format isn't the problem; the topology is. Even with JSON, the coordinator loses visibility and control.
The context cost is solved with lean, structured outputs, not by removing the point of control.
Critical findings are precisely the ones that need to go through the coordinator, which decides on redelegation and synthesis.

questoes.pergunta: While evaluating the synthesis, the Andrade & Teles coordinator notices there is nothing about lawsuits filed in 2024, even though the company went through a judicial reorganization reported in the news that year. What should it do?
opcoes: Run the whole pipeline again with the same request, to give the subagents another chance.
Ask the synthesis subagent to complete the 2024 section with whatever is most likely based on the news, clearly marking it as "estimated".
Redelegate a targeted query (2024, judicial reorganization) to the litigation subagent and re-synthesize.
Deliver the report as is, since the 2024 news may have no relevant legal impact.
questoes.explicacao: The coordinator evaluates, detects a gap, and redelegates in a targeted way.
feedbacks: Repeats everything, including what was already good, without directing the research at the gap.
Fills the gap with unsourced content, violating the rule that every claim has a source and a date.
Correct. Iterative refinement: run, evaluate, identify the gap, redelegate in a targeted way, and synthesize again.
A known gap left silent; at the very least it should be researched or noted.

questoes.pergunta: The Andrade & Teles coordinator, implemented with the Agent SDK, has an AgentDefinition for each of the four subagents, but never invokes them: it does all the searches itself and blows through its context. What is most likely missing?
opcoes: A configured SubagentStop hook, without which the SDK doesn't start subagents.
Instructing "always delegate when possible" in the coordinator's prompt, because the model doesn't delegate by default.
The WebSearch tool on the coordinator, so it knows when a search is large enough to delegate.
The Agent tool in the coordinator's allowedTools list, which is how it creates subagents.
questoes.explicacao: The coordinator needs Agent in allowedTools to spawn subagents.
feedbacks: SubagentStop reacts to a subagent finishing; it is not a prerequisite for creating them.
It may even help with the decision, but without the Agent tool available there is no way to delegate.
Giving the coordinator more search tools reinforces the problem: it will search on its own.
Correct. Subagents are created through the Agent tool (formerly Task); without it in allowedTools, the coordinator can't delegate.

questoes.pergunta: In the Andrade & Teles system, the litigation subagent's search_court_records tool sometimes returns a 503. Currently the subagent passes along "Search failed" and the coordinator aborts the entire report. Which changes are correct? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: The subagent performs a local retry with backoff on transient errors and only propagates to the coordinator what it couldn't resolve.
On a 503, the subagent returns an empty list of lawsuits with a success status, so the report proceeds without blocking and the partners receive it on time.
The coordinator, upon receiving any error, automatically redoes the entire report from scratch.
Standardize the error as "Operation failed" with isError true for all subagents.
Propagate a structured error (category, query attempted, partial results), and the coordinator proceeds with the partial results, noting the gap.
questoes.explicacao: Local retry for transient errors + structured propagation with partial results; never abort everything or stay silent.
feedbacks: Correct. Local recovery from transient errors avoids bothering the coordinator with failures that disappear within seconds.
Silent suppression (anti-pattern 7): the report would say "no lawsuits" based on a search that never ran.
Wastes all the successful work because of a single step; it's the expensive variant of aborting.
Standardized, but generic (anti-pattern 6): without a category or the attempted query, the coordinator doesn't know what to do.
Correct. An error with context enables a decision; not aborting the workflow over one step preserves the rest of the work.

questoes.pergunta: The Andrade & Teles news subagent uses the server-side web fetch tool. It tries to fetch URLs that it "infers" (for example, by constructing the address of a court's web page), and the calls fail. What is the explanation and the fix?
opcoes: The web fetch max_uses limit was reached; increase it to allow more fetches per request.
Server-side tools can't access court websites due to a security restriction; replace it with an internally hosted scraping MCP server.
Web fetch only accesses URLs already present in the conversation; bring them in first via web search or through the prompt.
The failure comes with stop_reason "pause_turn"; just resend the response to continue.
questoes.explicacao: Web fetch only fetches URLs already present in the conversation.
feedbacks: The symptom isn't a quota; it's that the URL isn't present in the conversation.
There's no such restriction by type of site; switching stacks attacks the wrong problem.
Correct. Web fetch is not a crawler; the URL must be present in the context, coming from the user, the prompt, or a search result.
pause_turn indicates the server-side loop's iteration ceiling, not an invalid URL.

questoes.pergunta: The Andrade & Teles news subagent performs many server-side searches in a single request. Some responses come back with stop_reason "pause_turn" and the code treats it as the end, delivering incomplete findings. What should be done?
opcoes: Treat pause_turn as a transient error and redo the original request from scratch with backoff.
Resend the conversation with the paused response appended, so the model continues.
Increase max_tokens, because pause_turn indicates the output was cut off.
Treat it as a safety refusal and log the query for manual review.
questoes.explicacao: pause_turn → resend to continue; it's not an error, a cutoff, or a refusal.
feedbacks: Throws away the progress already made and may hit the same ceiling again.
Correct. pause_turn means the server-side loop hit its iteration ceiling; resending the response lets the work continue.
That's stop_reason max_tokens, a different case. Confusing the two is the trap.
A refusal is stop_reason "refusal". pause_turn is operational, not safety-related.

questoes.pergunta: In the Andrade & Teles synthesis, the target company's annual report states revenue of R$ 412 million, while a news article cites R$ 380 million. Which practices should the synthesis subagent follow? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Use the average of the two values, R$ 396 million, indicating that it is a reconciled estimate.
Choose the annual report because it is an audited primary source and omit the news article from the text, so as not to confuse the partners with a less reliable number.
Check each number's reference date before calling it a conflict; different periods don't contradict each other.
If the conflict is real, present both values with their sources and dates, flagging the point as disputed.
Always choose the most recent value by publication date, recording only that source.
questoes.explicacao: Conflict: check the period; if it's real, show both with source and date. Never an average or a silent choice.
feedbacks: Averaging creates a number that no source stated; it's exactly what you should not do.
Choosing silently hides the divergence that the firm's rule requires surfacing.
Correct. Temporal data: record "data as of", publication, and collection dates. Many "contradictions" are just different periods.
Correct. A conflict is annotated with its sources; the partners decide with complete information.
A mechanical, silent criterion; the most recent publication may cite an older fiscal year.

questoes.pergunta: The Andrade & Teles subagents return summaries in running prose. In the final synthesis, the partners can't tell where each claim came from. What is the best fix?
opcoes: Ask the synthesis subagent, at the end, to search again for the sources of each claim and add a complete bibliography section.
Structured findings per subagent: claim, evidence, source, date, and source type, preserved in the synthesis.
Attach each subagent's full transcripts to the report as an audit appendix.
Instruct the subagents to write "according to public sources" before each claim.
questoes.explicacao: Provenance: claim + evidence + source + date, structured, preserved all the way to the synthesis.
feedbacks: Reconstructing sources afterward is expensive and prone to misattribution; provenance should travel with the finding.
Correct. Separating content from metadata lets attribution survive aggregation.
Volume is not provenance: nobody can map claim → source across thousands of lines.
Vague attribution doesn't identify a document or a date; it doesn't meet the firm's rule.

questoes.pergunta: The Andrade & Teles synthesis subagent receives 130,000 tokens of concatenated subagent outputs. Relevant findings that were in the middle of that block don't appear in the report. What is the best approach?
opcoes: Migrate the synthesis to a model with a larger context window, so that all the subagents' material fits with plenty of room and nothing is truncated.
Repeat at the end of the prompt: "read all the material carefully, including what's in the middle".
Enable context editing with clear_tool_uses on the synthesis subagent.
Lean, structured outputs from the subagents, with key findings at the beginning and section headers.
questoes.explicacao: Lost in the middle: cut the volume, put the critical content at the beginning, use headers.
feedbacks: Fitting isn't the problem; the model already receives everything. A larger window tends to make lost in the middle worse.
A generic instruction doesn't change how attention is distributed across a huge, unstructured block.
The synthesis has no tool history to clear; the material arrives in the prompt. The right tool for a different problem.
Correct. Attacks lost in the middle from two sides: less volume, and the critical content at the beginning, with structure.

questoes.pergunta: The Andrade & Teles team is prototyping the workflow in Claude Code and created the /due-diligence skill, which performs dozens of searches and reads many documents. After it is used, the main conversation is flooded with search output. Which adjustment solves this?
opcoes: Add disable-model-invocation: true, so the skill only runs when invoked manually.
Add context: fork to the frontmatter, running the skill in an isolated subagent.
Move the skill's content into the project's CLAUDE.md so it's always available.
Run /compact right after each use of the skill to clean up the conversation.
questoes.explicacao: Heavy, noisy skill → context: fork (isolated subagent).
feedbacks: Controls who can invoke it, not where the output ends up; the conversation stays flooded.
Correct. context: fork runs the skill in a subagent with its own context; the search noise stays inside it.
It would load the procedure into every session and would still execute in the main context.
A reactive remedy that loses details; the right approach is not to let the noise into the main context in the first place.

questoes.pergunta: The Andrade & Teles analysis subagent classifies risks as "high", "medium", or "low" with the instruction "use your good legal judgment". The same labor lawsuit receives different classifications in different runs. What is the best fix?
opcoes: Ask the model to report its confidence in each classification and discard those below 0.7.
Explicit criteria per level (what counts, what doesn't) with boundary examples.
Run the classification three times and adopt the majority.
Add "be conservative when classifying risks" to the prompt.
questoes.explicacao: Explicit criteria + boundary examples beat "use your good judgment".
feedbacks: Self-reported confidence isn't calibrated and doesn't define what "high" is; it only filters at random.
Correct. Explicit criteria with borderline cases are what produce consistency; "good judgment" produces variation.
More expensive, and it only stabilizes around a criterion that remains undefined.
The same vagueness as "good judgment"; it doesn't say where the boundary lies.

questoes.pergunta: The Andrade & Teles litigation subagent extracts the case number, court division, and amount in controversy from court docket entries. When the amount in controversy doesn't appear in the document, it invents a plausible value. Which use of few-shot helps the most?
opcoes: Twenty examples of complete docket entries, all with the amount in controversy present, to reinforce the format.
A single perfect example, so as not to induce the model to copy details from the examples.
No examples; just the instruction "do not invent values", highlighted.
2 to 4 varied examples with reasoning, including one with the amount missing and a null output.
questoes.explicacao: Few-shot: 2–4 varied examples with reasoning, including the edge case.
feedbacks: Many identical examples teach that the field always exists, reinforcing the invention.
One example doesn't cover the edge cases; the missing-value case still has no demonstration.
Helps little without showing the expected behavior or a field that accepts null.
Correct. Targeted few-shot, with reasoning and covering the edge case, teaches the "missing → null" pattern.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: Hospital Santa Aurora maintains a monorepo with its electronic health record system (.NET backend and Angular frontend). The platform team integrated Claude Code into the GitHub Actions pipeline to review PRs, generate tests, and run a nightly security audit. Constraints: patient data (LGPD) must never appear in logs or comments; the PR review must finish in under 10 minutes because it blocks the merge; the job cannot change the repository without going through a PR; the monthly API budget is fixed.

Santa Aurora's first job runs claude "review this PR" on the runner and hangs until the GitHub Actions 6-hour timeout. What is the fix?
opcoes: Add --max-turns 5 so the session ends after a few iterations.
Use --permission-mode bypassPermissions so that no approval stalls the job.
Run in non-interactive mode with -p (--print), passing the prompt and the CI flags.
Set the CI=true environment variable so that Claude Code detects the pipeline.
questoes.explicacao: In CI, -p is mandatory; without it the process hangs waiting for input.
feedbacks: Limits the turns of a run, but the interactive session keeps waiting for the user.
Addresses permission prompts, not the interactive session; and it's dangerous as a routine practice.
Correct. Without -p, Claude Code opens an interactive session and waits for input that never comes.
That isn't the mechanism for non-interactive operation; print mode is made explicit with -p.

questoes.pergunta: Santa Aurora's review job needs to produce output that a script turns into inline PR comments (file, line, severity, message). Currently the prompt asks to "respond in JSON" and parsing fails in 4% of runs. What is the best approach?
opcoes: Keep the request in prose and add a regex that extracts the first block between curly braces from the response.
--output-format json with --json-schema describing the list of findings.
Use --output-format stream-json and concatenate the text events to build the final JSON.
Repeat the run until parsing succeeds, with at most five attempts.
questoes.explicacao: CI output meant for machines: --output-format json + --json-schema.
feedbacks: A fragile patch: it still depends on well-formed free text.
Correct. Guarantees schema-compliant output instead of depending on the text coming out well formed.
stream-json is for following events; it doesn't impose a schema on the content.
Blind retries that don't attack the cause cost time out of the 10-minute budget, and money.

questoes.pergunta: The Santa Aurora team wants to cut costs by using the Batch API. Which workloads are suitable for it? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: The nightly security audit over the backend's 1,200 files, read the following morning.
The PR review that blocks the merge and must finish in under 10 minutes.
The job that fixes failing tests by iterating with Read, Edit, and Bash until they pass.
The weekly technical debt report per module, consolidated every Monday.
The review of a production hotfix that must be merged within 15 minutes.
questoes.explicacao: Batch: bulk, no deadline, no multi-turn. Never pre-merge/blocking.
feedbacks: Correct. A bulk workload with no immediate deadline: it fits within the up-to-24h window with a 50% discount.
Batch has no SLA and can take up to 24h; never use it in a blocking CI step.
Requires a multi-turn tool loop, which the Batch API doesn't support within a request.
Correct. Periodic, delay-tolerant, and non-interactive: a typical batch profile.
Urgent and blocking; the discount doesn't make up for a window with no guarantee.

questoes.pergunta: At Santa Aurora, a job generates unit tests with Claude and, in the same session, asks "now review the tests you wrote". The review approves almost everything, but the team finds tests that only verify their own mock. What should change?
opcoes: Keep the same session, but replace the review prompt with a stricter one that has a detailed checklist.
Resume the generation session with --resume and request the review after an interval.
Review in a new session that receives only the diff and the quality criteria.
Raise the generation session's effort so the tests come out better from the start and the review becomes unnecessary.
questoes.explicacao: Review in a new session: the session that wrote the code doesn't review it.
feedbacks: A checklist helps, but in the same session the bias remains (anti-pattern 9).
Resuming loads exactly the same biased context.
Correct. Whoever generated the code won't question its own decisions; an independent session removes the bias of the reasoning context.
Improving generation is good, but it doesn't replace independent review.

questoes.pergunta: A Santa Aurora PR changed 38 files (controllers, services, DTOs, Angular components). The single-pass review missed a broken contract between a DTO and a component and commented on the same pattern in contradictory ways in different files. Which strategy fixes this?
opcoes: Pass 1 per file; pass 2, with a separate prompt, cross-checks the findings for integration.
Use a model with a larger window so that all 38 files fit in one pass with room to spare.
Run the same single-pass review three times and merge the comments.
Split the PR among three reviewers who analyze groups of files and post their comments directly.
questoes.explicacao: Large PR: per-file pass + integration pass.
feedbacks: Correct. Multi-pass review avoids attention dilution and inconsistency, and the integration pass catches the cross-file bug.
Fitting doesn't solve attention dilution; the problem is the design of the review, not the size of the window.
Triples the cost and repeats the same dilution; it still produces contradictory comments.
Improves the local view, but nobody looks at the integration between groups: the broken contract still gets through.

questoes.pergunta: Santa Aurora's review job should be read-only, but in two runs Claude edited files "to fix the problem". Which configuration solves this deterministically?
opcoes: Add "never edit files" via --append-system-prompt.
Run with --permission-mode acceptEdits, so that the edits get recorded in the log.
--allowedTools with only Read, Grep, and Glob, and --disallowedTools for Edit, Write, and Bash.
Reduce --max-turns to 3, so there are no turns left for editing.
questoes.explicacao: Read-only in CI → restrict the tools; don't rely on the prompt.
feedbacks: Probabilistic: it reduces edits but doesn't prevent them (anti-pattern 3).
acceptEdits approves edits automatically; it's the opposite of what's wanted.
Correct. The tool restriction is enforced by the harness; the model can't even edit.
A turn limit doesn't prevent an edit right at the start and may cut the review short.

questoes.pergunta: Santa Aurora's reviews ignore team conventions (use ILogger with structured messages, never log patient data). The conventions exist in the tech lead's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, where they work well locally. What is the cause and the fix?
opcoes: The runner doesn't have the user's CLAUDE.md; move the conventions to the project's CLAUDE.md.
Move the conventions to CLAUDE.local.md at the root, which is loaded in any environment.
Copy the conventions into Claude Code's auto memory (MEMORY.md) on the runner.
Pass the content of the tech lead's file via --append-system-prompt, reading it from a GitHub secret.
questoes.explicacao: Team rule → project CLAUDE.md, version-controlled.
feedbacks: Correct. The user CLAUDE.md is personal; team rules go at the project level, version-controlled with the code.
CLAUDE.local.md is personal and gitignored; it doesn't reach the runner.
Auto memory is local to the machine and not version-controlled; it's not where team rules should live.
Works poorly: it duplicates the source of truth outside the repository and doesn't benefit developers locally.

questoes.pergunta: In Santa Aurora's monorepo, test projects are scattered (src/*/Tests, libs/*/Tests, and new modules appear every month). The team wants the testing conventions (xUnit, naming, AAA) to load only when Claude works on test files. What is the best option?
opcoes: A CLAUDE.md inside each test directory with the same conventions, created as new modules appear.
A large section in the root CLAUDE.md with all the testing conventions.
A file in .claude/rules/ with paths: frontmatter pointing to the glob of the test files.
A /test-conventions skill that developers invoke when they remember to.
questoes.explicacao: A convention that spans directories → .claude/rules/ with paths.
feedbacks: Duplicates content and doesn't automatically cover the modules that will appear.
Loads in every session, even when no tests are involved; it wastes context.
Correct. A path-scoped rule covers current and future directories and only loads when matching files are touched.
Depends on someone remembering; it's not automatic path-based loading.

questoes.pergunta: Santa Aurora's review posts comments in four categories. The "style" category has 60% false positives, and developers have started ignoring all comments, including the security ones, which are accurate. What is the best action?
opcoes: Keep all the categories and add "be conservative with style comments".
Display only comments with self-reported confidence above 0.8, in all categories.
Downgrade style comments to "suggestion" without changing the criterion that generates them.
Turn off "style", refine the criterion with boundary examples, and only then turn it back on.
questoes.explicacao: Noisy category: turn it off, refine it with explicit criteria, turn it back on.
feedbacks: Vague; it doesn't define the boundary, and the noise continues.
Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated; it may cut out true security findings.
Changes the label, not the quality; developers keep learning to ignore the bot.
Correct. A noisy category erodes trust in the good ones; turn it off, refine it with explicit criteria, turn it back on.

questoes.pergunta: Santa Aurora's dashboard shows that 94% of the automated review's comments were accepted by developers this quarter. The security team is suspicious of its quality on EF Core migrations. Which actions are appropriate? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Break the metric down by finding category and by file type (migrations, controllers, components) before concluding that the review is good.
Uniformly increase the audited sample from 2% to 10% of all PRs.
Build the human audit sample stratified by risk, with a higher rate for migrations and code that touches patient data.
Keep the process, since 94% acceptance proves the quality of the review.
Ask Claude to include its confidence from 0 to 1 in each comment and focus human auditing only on the comments flagged with low confidence.
questoes.explicacao: Disaggregate the metric and stratify sampling by risk.
feedbacks: Correct. An aggregate metric hides per-segment failures (anti-pattern 10).
A larger uniform sample spends effort where risk is low and may underrepresent migrations.
Correct. Stratified sampling concentrates review where errors cost the most.
Aggregate acceptance doesn't measure false negatives or quality per file type.
Self-reported confidence isn't calibrated; it's no substitute for risk-based stratification.

questoes.pergunta: Santa Aurora needs to guarantee that Claude, in CI, never runs git push and never reads appsettings.Production.json (connection strings). What is the most appropriate implementation?
opcoes: A rule in the project's CLAUDE.md: "never push and never read production files".
A PostToolUse hook that detects the push or the read and reverts the action.
The same PreToolUse hook, configured in .claude/settings.local.json so as not to expose the blocking logic in the repository.
A PreToolUse hook in the version-controlled .claude/settings.json, blocking these patterns before execution.
questoes.explicacao: Security → PreToolUse blocking beforehand, in version-controlled project settings.
feedbacks: A prompt is probabilistic (anti-pattern 3); security needs deterministic blocking.
Too late: the file's content has already entered the context and the push has already gone out.
settings.local.json is gitignored; it doesn't reach the CI runner.
Correct. A security rule in code, before execution, configured at the project level so it applies to every run.

questoes.pergunta: A Santa Aurora job fixes failing tests. On the next run, it uses --resume on the previous session, but between the two runs a developer pushed changes to 6 of the files involved, and Claude starts editing based on the old content. What should be done?
opcoes: A new session with a structured summary of what was done, stating explicitly which files changed.
Continue with --resume, because the history helps Claude remember the previous attempts.
Use --fork-session from the previous session so as not to contaminate it.
Run /compact on the resumed session before continuing.
questoes.explicacao: The world changed → new session + structured summary + what changed.
feedbacks: Correct. Resuming is worthwhile when the tool results are still valid; files changed, so start fresh with a summary and say what changed.
The history contains reads of files that no longer exist in that form; the model acts on stale data.
The fork inherits the same outdated history; it protects the original but doesn't fix the problem.
Compressing old results doesn't make them current; and it still doesn't say what changed.

questoes.pergunta: Santa Aurora's nightly audit sometimes enters long cycles, and one run reached 180 turns. What is the correct role of --max-turns (and of a budget cap) in this job?
opcoes: To be the main termination mechanism: set 20 turns so that the job always ends at that point.
Use no limit, because the model decides when to stop and any cap interferes with the result.
A backstop against runaway runs; termination comes from a bounded task with a clear criterion.
Replace the limit with an instruction in the prompt: "finish in at most 20 steps".
questoes.explicacao: --max-turns/budget = backstop, not the main mechanism.
feedbacks: Anti-pattern 2: an arbitrary limit as the main criterion cuts off valid work or lets incomplete work pass as if it were done.
Without a backstop, a cycle eats up the fixed budget; that's what the limit is for.
Correct. An iteration limit is a valid backstop; the main mechanism is a clear task and criterion.
A prompt is not a reliable cap; and the model doesn't precisely control how many turns it will use.

questoes.pergunta: At Santa Aurora, the audit job needs to find all uses of a deprecated method (PatientRepository.GetRaw). The first version read all 1,200 files and blew through the context. What is the correct approach?
opcoes: Grep for the method name, read only the files found, and follow the imports as needed.
Glob on **/*.cs to list all the C# files and read each result, filtering those that actually call the deprecated method.
First read all the files in the Data/ directory, then the rest if there's context left.
Migrate the job to a model with a 1M window so that the 1,200 files fit.
questoes.explicacao: Codebase: grep for the entry points, read only what's relevant.
feedbacks: Correct. Incremental exploration: grep → read → follow → read. It spends context only on what's relevant.
Glob locates files by name, not by content; reading everything is the same anti-pattern.
It's still reading up front, betting on a hypothesis about where the usage is.
Expensive on every turn and worsens lost in the middle; the problem is the strategy.

questoes.pergunta: The Santa Aurora team asks Claude Code for a date parser for medical records (formats "dd/MM/yyyy", "dd/MM/yy HH:mm", and partial dates like "03/2024"). Prose descriptions produce implementations that get the edge cases wrong on every attempt. What is the most effective approach?
opcoes: TDD: failing tests with concrete examples (including partial dates), iterating until they pass.
Rewrite the prose specification with more detail about each format.
Ask Claude to generate five different implementations and pick the one that seems best.
Use plan mode so that Claude designs the parser's architecture before coding.
questoes.explicacao: Iterative refinement: concrete examples and TDD.
feedbacks: Correct. Concrete examples and TDD provide a verifiable target; they outperform prose descriptions.
More prose keeps the ambiguity that is already failing.
No objective selection criterion; expensive and doesn't converge.
Plan mode is for broad changes; what's missing here is a concrete target, not architecture.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: Conecta Insumos, a B2B marketplace for industrial supplies, receives about 40,000 documents per month from suppliers: PDF invoices, purchase orders, technical reports, and delivery receipts (some handwritten and scanned). A pipeline with Claude extracts the data as JSON and loads it into the ERP. Constraints: the ERP rejects invalid records; missing data must not be invented; financial reconciliation requires exact amounts; the cost per document must drop 30% this year.

Currently the prompt asks to "respond only with valid JSON" and about 3% of the outputs come back malformed or missing required fields. Conecta uses a recent model. What is the best fix?
opcoes: Prefill the assistant response with "{" to force the start of a JSON object.
Add a step that fixes malformed JSON with regex and fills in missing fields with default values.
Structured outputs (output_config.format) or an extraction tool with strict: true.
Repeat the call until the JSON parses, with at most five attempts.
questoes.explicacao: Structured output: structured outputs or a tool with strict.
feedbacks: Prefill returns a 400 on newer models; and even where it works, it doesn't guarantee fields and types.
A patch that invents data when it fills fields with defaults, violating the constraint.
Correct. Schema compliance guaranteed by the API, instead of depending on well-formed free text.
Blind retries cost more and don't attack the cause.

questoes.pergunta: At Conecta, with structured outputs enabled, 100% of the outputs pass the schema, but on 2.5% of the invoices total_amount doesn't match the sum of the line items and the ERP rejects them. What is the best approach?
opcoes: Nothing to do in the pipeline: strict guarantees the data; the discrepancies are the supplier's error.
Add "check that the total matches the sum of the items" to the prompt.
Raise effort to "max" on all extractions to reduce reading errors.
Validate the sum and dates in code and, if validation fails, retry with the specific errors.
questoes.explicacao: Valid schema ≠ correct semantics: validate in code + retry with the specific error.
feedbacks: Strict guarantees shape, not arithmetic. Some of the discrepancies are misreadings by the model.
Helps, but it's best-effort; the deterministically correct check is in code.
Makes all 40,000 documents more expensive without detecting the cases that fail.
Correct. Schema compliance ≠ semantic correctness; validate in code and retry with the specific error.

questoes.pergunta: At Conecta, many invoices don't include the purchase order number. The schema requires purchase_order as a string, and the model fills it with plausible numbers that then don't exist in the ERP. What is the fix?
opcoes: Keep the field required and add a retry loop until the model finds the number.
Add a regex pattern to the strict schema to accept only the real order format.
Make purchase_order nullable and instruct the model to return null when it isn't in the document.
Include few-shot examples in which invoices without an order appear with an order number filled in.
questoes.explicacao: Data that may be missing → nullable field; a retry doesn't create information.
feedbacks: A retry doesn't recover information that isn't in the source; it just produces another invention.

A simple `pattern` is in fact supported in strict, but it only guarantees format: an invented number in the right format would pass. It doesn't attack the cause (a required field with no way to say "there isn't one").
Correct. A nullable field gives the model a legitimate way to say "there isn't one"; requiring a string forces invention.
Teaches exactly the wrong behavior.

questoes.pergunta: Conecta's validation loop, on failure, resends the same prompt with "the previous result was invalid, try again". The success rate on the second attempt barely changes. What should be improved?
opcoes: Increase the maximum number of retries from 2 to 6.
Switch models on each retry, alternating between two models.
Retry with the specific errors (field, value, rule) and, at the limit, an explicit failure for review.
At the attempt limit, write the last output to the ERP with a "low confidence" flag.
questoes.explicacao: A useful retry = specific errors in the prompt + a limit + explicit failure.
feedbacks: More attempts without new information repeat the same error, at a higher cost.
Complexity without attacking the cause: neither model knows what was wrong.
Correct. A specific error guides the correction; a limit with explicit failure avoids loops and bad data in the ERP.
Writes data known to be invalid; the constraint is not to load invalid records.

questoes.pergunta: Conecta's document_type field is an enum of 6 values. New suppliers send documents that don't fit (e.g., an electronic correction letter), and they end up forced into "invoice". What is the best schema adjustment?
opcoes: Add "other" with a detail field and "unclear" for ambiguous documents.
Turn the field into a free-form string to accept any type.
Add to the prompt "choose the closest category whenever you're not sure".
Create an enum with 40 values covering every existing tax document.
questoes.explicacao: Enum: "other" + detail and "unclear" so the model doesn't guess.
feedbacks: Correct. An enum with an "other" + detail option and "unclear" keeps the model from guessing the closest category.
Loses the validation and standardization that the ERP needs.
Makes guessing official, which is exactly the problem.
Bloated, still finite, and it increases confusion between neighboring values.

questoes.pergunta: Conecta wants to detect invoices in which the reading, or the document itself, is inconsistent before reconciliation. Which practices help? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Rely on the schema's strict: true, which already rejects out-of-range numeric values, impossible dates, and contradictions between related fields.
Extract the amount stated on the document and also calculate the amount from the line items in code, flagging any discrepancy.
Validate contradictions between fields in code, such as a due date earlier than the issue date or an issuer CNPJ that doesn't exist in the registry.
Ask the model for an overall_confidence field from 0 to 1 and reconcile only documents above 0.9.
Use minLength and pattern in the strict schema to guarantee the CNPJ format.
questoes.explicacao: Stated vs. calculated + semantic validation in code.
feedbacks: Strict doesn't support numeric ranges or cross-field logic.
Correct. Stated vs. calculated amounts reveal a reading error or a document error.
Correct. Semantic validation and validation of referenced entities are done in code.
Self-reported confidence isn't calibrated; it doesn't detect the concrete discrepancy.
`minLength` is not supported by strict (400 on the raw schema); a simple `pattern` would work, but it only guarantees the CNPJ format and doesn't detect an inconsistent reading or document.

questoes.pergunta: Conecta processes its monthly backlog through the Batch API. The script matched each result to its document by position in the results list, and several invoices ended up with other invoices' data. In addition, 3% of the requests came back as errored. What is the correct procedure?
opcoes: Sort the results by completion time to reconstruct the submission order.
Match by custom_id and resubmit only the custom_ids that failed.
Resubmit the entire batch whenever there are errored results, to keep the order consistent.
Switch to synchronous calls, which preserve order and have no errors.
questoes.explicacao: Batch: match by custom_id; resubmit only the ones that failed.
feedbacks: There's no guarantee that completion follows submission order; it's still fragile.
Correct. Results may come back out of order; custom_id is the key. Reprocess only the ones that failed.
Pays again for the 97% that succeeded and doesn't fix the matching by position.
Loses the 50% discount, going against the cost goal; synchronous calls fail too.

questoes.pergunta: Conecta's extraction tool was marked with strict: true, and the API started rejecting the definition. The input_schema has 14 properties, only 9 of them in required, and it doesn't declare additionalProperties. What is the correct adjustment?
opcoes: Remove the 5 optional properties from the schema, keeping only the required ones.
Declare additionalProperties: false; the 5 optional ones can stay, but ideally they should be in required as nullable.
Declare additionalProperties: true to allow the optional ones.
Give up on strict and validate everything in code, since strict doesn't work with optional fields.
questoes.explicacao: Strict requires additionalProperties: false on every object. Optional properties are allowed (they count toward a per-request limit [volatile]); the recommendation is required + nullable.
feedbacks: Loses data the business needs when that data exists.
Correct. What's missing is additionalProperties: false. Optional properties don't prevent strict, but required + nullable makes absence explicit.
The opposite of strict's requirement.
False premise: strict accepts optional properties (within a limit); giving it up is unnecessary.

questoes.pergunta: When migrating Conecta's pipeline to a newer model, calls with tool_choice {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_invoice"} started returning HTTP 400. The forcing existed only to get JSON in the schema's format. What is the best way forward?
opcoes: Switch to tool_choice "any", which has the same effect with fewer restrictions.
Permanently go back to the previous model, since the request shape became incompatible with the new API version.
Use tool_choice "none" and ask for the JSON in free text.
Structured outputs with the same schema (or auto + instruction + strict), testing the request.
questoes.explicacao: Forcing a tool to get JSON → structured outputs on newer models.
feedbacks: On those same models, "any" is also rejected.
Abandons the migration over a simple adjustment.
Goes back to the malformed JSON problem that forcing solved.
Correct. On newer models, forcing can return a 400; if the goal was JSON, structured outputs is the direct path.

questoes.pergunta: Conecta wants to share with the whole team the ERP's remote MCP server (HTTP with a token) used while developing the pipeline with Claude Code. Which practices are correct? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Declare only the url, without type, because Claude Code infers HTTP when there is a url.
Declare the server in .mcp.json at the repository root with "type": "http" and the url.
Configure it in the MCP local scope, in .claude/settings.local.json, so that it is shared with the team.
Commit the literal token in .mcp.json, since the repository is private.
Put the token in headers as "Bearer ${ERP_TOKEN}", with the variable defined in each developer's environment.
questoes.explicacao: .mcp.json with an explicit type + secrets via ${VAR}.
feedbacks: Trap: without type, the entry is read as stdio and fails.
Correct. Project scope, shared via git; a remote server needs a declared type.
Double confusion: the local scope lives in ~/.claude.json and isn't shared; it isn't settings.local.json either.
A secret in a version-controlled file leaks with the history; a private repository doesn't change that.
Correct. Secrets via variable expansion, never literal in the version-controlled file.

questoes.pergunta: At Conecta, the /reprocess-batch <date> skill triggers an expensive batch and writes control files. The team noticed that Claude invokes it on its own when someone merely mentions "batch" in the conversation. Which frontmatter adjustment solves this?
opcoes: user-invocable: false, to remove it from the command menu.
disable-model-invocation: true, leaving the skill for manual invocation only.
context: fork, so that the execution is isolated in a subagent.
Rewrite the description to make it vaguer, reducing the chances of it being auto-loaded.
questoes.explicacao: Skill with side effects → disable-model-invocation: true.
feedbacks: Does the opposite: hides it from the user and keeps invocation by the model.
Correct. A skill with costly side effects should be invocable only manually.
Isolates the context, but doesn't prevent automatic invocation.
Probabilistic, and it makes the documentation worse; the deterministic control exists.

questoes.pergunta: Conecta is going to migrate 45 extraction prompts, spread across several services, from forced tool_choice to structured outputs, adjusting schemas, validations, and tests. How should Claude Code be used?
opcoes: Direct execution file by file, requesting each conversion as the files are found.
Run in bypassPermissions to speed up the 45 edits without interruptions.
Create a rule in .claude/rules/ saying "use structured outputs" and expect the edits to happen naturally.
Start in plan mode: explore the usages, propose the approach and migration order for approval, and only then edit.
questoes.explicacao: Large, multi-file change → plan mode.
feedbacks: Without a view of the whole, schema/validation decisions end up inconsistent across services.
Not a routine practice for a long change; it removes control exactly where it matters.
A rule guides future edits; it doesn't plan or execute a migration.
Correct. A multi-file change involving design decisions is the typical case for plan mode.

questoes.pergunta: Conecta's flow is always the same: classify the document type → extract with that type's schema → validate → load into the ERP. An engineer proposes replacing it with an autonomous agent that decides the steps for each document. What is the correct assessment?
opcoes: Keep prompt chaining: fixed, known steps are more predictable and cheaper.
Adopt the autonomous agent, because it handles new document types better.
Adopt a coordinator with a subagent for each step, talking to one another.
Keep the chain, but ask the model, at each step, to decide whether the next step is needed.
questoes.explicacao: Fixed, known steps → prompt chaining.
feedbacks: Correct. Dynamic decomposition is for open-ended investigation; fixed steps call for chaining.
New types are handled in the schema ("other"/"unclear"); autonomy here only adds variance.
Unnecessary complexity for a linear flow, and with direct communication between subagents.
Reintroduces dynamic decision-making where it adds nothing; validation and loading are always needed.

questoes.pergunta: Conecta has a coordinator with subagents for handwriting OCR, table extraction, technical reports, and invoices. Currently every document goes through all four, including simple digital PDFs. What is the best change?
opcoes: The coordinator classifies the document and invokes only the subagents that the document needs.
Run all four in parallel, so that the total time equals that of the slowest subagent.
Merge the four subagents into a single agent with all the tools.
Keep all of them, but send only the first page to the irrelevant subagents.
questoes.explicacao: The coordinator invokes only the necessary subagents.
feedbacks: Correct. Invoke only the subagents the task needs; the rest is cost and noise.
Improves the time, but keeps the cost of four runs per document.
Goes back to the problem of too many tools in one agent.
Still invokes what isn't needed; it only reduces the damage.

questoes.pergunta: Conecta wants to reduce human review by automatically approving documents in which the model declares "confidence: high" in an output field. What is the best approach?
opcoes: Automatically approve everything with "confidence: high", because the model knows its own uncertainty.
Require the model to justify high confidence and approve when the justification is convincing.
Per-field confidence calibrated on a labeled set + risk-stratified sampling.
Review 5% of all documents, drawn uniformly at random, and approve the rest.
questoes.explicacao: Calibrated per-field confidence + risk-stratified sampling.
feedbacks: Anti-pattern 4: self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated.
A convincing justification is not calibration; it's still self-reported.
Correct. Confidence only means something if it is calibrated; stratifying by risk directs review to where errors are most frequent.
A uniform sample underrepresents handwritten delivery receipts, where accuracy is usually much lower.
